In addition, AcHACS, a phylogenetically distant variant from RuHACS and other first-round HACS variants, also showed notable condensation activity (Figure 26D). Therefore, ApbHACS, BpbHACS, DhcHACS, and AcHACS were used as references to identify 99 second-round HACS variants, using an approach described for the first-round variants. Learnings from the sequence and structure analyses presented in previous sections were applied to narrow down variants with a higher chance of encoding acyloin condensation activity (i.e., high active site sequence similarity with active variants) and eliminating OXC variants that showed no HACS activity based on the characteristic active site residues. Moreover, we explored enzymes that have structural similarity irrespective of the sequence similarity using I-TASSER (Morrison & Weiss, 2001), which yielded nine additional variants. Of the total 108 genes identified, genes encoding 99 HACS variants were successfully synthesized and constructed into plasmids for testing following the same procedure described for screening of first-round variants (Figure 26A-C). A total of 134 variants including known enzymes from the HACS/OXC family (RuHACS, AcHACS, EcOXC, OfOXC, MeOXC and MeOXC4), the first (HACS-1-1 to 29), and second round (99 successful variants from HACS-2-1 to 108) HACS variants were organized in a sequence similarity network (SSN) (Yang et al., 2015) with the heatmap 41 showing relative glycolate fluxes (Figure 28A-B). Clustering variants by connecting nodes with 50% and higher sequence identity resulted in three large clusters (Figure 28A): the biggest cluster labeled as RuHACS cluster that includes all HACS variants related to active variants from the first round (RuHACS, ApbHACS, BpbHACS and DhcHACS); a medium cluster representing AcHACS cluster identified from the second round; and a small cluster for OXC variants which include EcOXC, OfOXC, MeOXC and variants with characteristic sequences of OXCs identified from the first round variants (Figure 26D). Remarkably, variants showing activities are only found from the two large clusters, except for MeOXC424 and HACS-2-76, which do not belong to any clusters (Figure 28A). When a more stringent identity threshold of 70% was imposed, the RuHACS cluster was divided into subclusters, including a RuHACS-ApbHACS cluster, a DhcHACS cluster, and a third cluster harboring highly active new variants with none of the active variants from the first round (Figure 28B). More than half of the variants in the DhcHACS cluster show good activity, including HACS-2-25, which showed 30% increase in glycolate flux compared to DhcHACS (Figure 28B-C). Interestingly, HACS-2- 65 (HACS from Chloroflexi bacterium HGW-Chloroflexi-9, CfhHACS), which stands out among all variants with close to a two-fold higher glycolate flux than DhcHACS, belongs to the third cluster (CfhHACS cluster) indicating lower than 70% sequence identity with active first round variants (Figure 28B-C).
